title: T1567.002 — Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
subtitle: Interactive walkthrough of Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration to Cloud Storage with the technique-specific attack path and defender evidence.
aria: T1567.002 - Exfiltration Over Web Service - Exfiltration to Cloud Storage

steps.title: Quiet before the storm
steps.caption: FS01 was compromised days earlier through a stolen VPN account for a backup vendor; a scheduled-task implant is active but idle. The attacker only beacons gently to blend in. Evidence: VPN login from a new ASN (autonomous system number, the network’s identifier); one new scheduled task on FS01
steps.defender: almost nothing in the moment - the only clue is one odd VPN login from a new country weeks ago, closed as a false positive.

steps.title: Shopping for data
steps.caption: From the implant, the attacker sweeps the shares: dir /s walks over finance, HR and R&D folders to build a target list. Evidence: EDR process lines full of dir sweeps; off-hours share enumeration
steps.defender: the EDR records a burst of around 1,400 directory listings in twelve minutes - at 03:00 local time, from a server that normally only serves files.

steps.title: Packing with a password
steps.caption: The attacker compresses the chosen shares into one archive: 7z a -p C:\Windows\Temp\arc.7z \\FS01\finance (shown for lab practice only). A single password-protected file is far easier to upload than ten thousand small ones. 7z.exe runs on a server for the first time ever, and a temp file starts growing toward gigabytes. Evidence: 7z first-seen on FS01; arc.7z growing in C:\Windows\Temp

steps.title: The remote config appears
steps.caption: rclone is staged and configured: rclone config writes a remote named mega: into %APPDATA%\rclone\rclone.conf , holding the attacker’s cloud credentials. rclone.conf - a filename that has never appeared anywhere in the estate - and the first execution of rclone.exe on record. Evidence: Sysmon 11 create of rclone.conf; rclone.exe never seen before

steps.title: The upload
steps.caption: The main event: rclone copy C:\Windows\Temp mega:corp-backup pushes tens of gigabytes out, split across parallel TLS connections and shaped with --bwlimit to stay polite. Evidence: proxy bytes-up baseline break; CASB unmanaged-app event on mega.nz
steps.defender: the proxy’s per-host upload bytes explode to about 50× the 30-day baseline for FS01, and the CASB flags an unmanaged cloud-storage app. This alert is the real warning window.

steps.title: Cleaning up
steps.caption: The attacker deletes arc.7z , wipes the staging folder, and touches a few file timestamps to confuse later review. $STANDARD_INFORMATION and $FILE_NAME timestamps - a classic timestomping hint. Evidence: USN delete of arc.7z; EDR timestamp-mismatch flag

steps.title: Attacker downloads
steps.caption: On their own infrastructure, the attacker pulls the archive from Mega to keep a local copy. Evidence: no on-prem telemetry; provider account is attacker-controlled
steps.defender: nothing on the corporate side - the download happens entirely inside the cloud provider, between the attacker’s account and their devices. This is why cloud storage feels safe to attackers and why the earlier steps matter more.

detection.label: Alert raised
detection.detail: The SOC has enough evidence to open an incident.

steps.title: Encryption follows
steps.caption: With the data safely copied, the attacker runs the ransomware: shares get encrypted, a note appears, and the extortion email quotes samples of the stolen files. Evidence: encryption events (late); rclone alert timeline showing a ~6-hour lead
steps.defender: the SOC replay now shows the whole chain - and the rclone alert fired roughly six hours before the first encryption event. That gap was the warning window; this page exists to make sure it is never missed again.
